title: Explaining Mixtures of Sources in News Articles

reviews.summary:
The paper analyzes one part of writing planning, namely source selection.

They define metrics to select the most likely plan underlying a story, revealing standard features (e.g., stance, social affiliation) that correlate with source planning in general documents."

The task tackled can be helpful for journalists, or even for readers, to understand the nature of the sources used.
The paper's clarity has some room for improvement (see weaknesses).
reviews.strengths:
- The paper tackles a new task related to writing planning.

- The paper shows extensive experiments, and the authors promise to make their classifiers available, which could be a good addition to the community.

- The paper reveals some interesting insights (Section 5)
reviews.weaknesses:
- The paper has room for improvement to enhance its clarity:

    -  **Consistency**: For example, plan, schema, and approach explain the same thing - this is repeated for different things. 

    - In Figure 2, "label set" is used for labels, but in line 321, "category" is used.

    -  What does *t* refer to in line 322?

- An overview graph can help explain the different components of the paper.

- The authors describe a "plan" as the set of labels in an article for one schema type (red circles or blue squares) (e.g., Affiliation, Stance), as depicted in Figure 1. What if a "plan" is a combination of both a square and a circle? 

- Two annotators annotated the dataset: Given that the agreement is moderate, how did they solve disagreements? 

- An overview (using descriptive statistics) can help understand the data, such as the distribution of schema labels per news article type in the "silver-standard dataset" and the dataset used for the main experiments.

reviews.summary:
Summary:
This paper introduces a schema ontology for news articles. They also propose metrics to study how well a schema structure explains a given news article. This is motivated by trying to computationally understand and potentially be able to replicate how humans (journalists) plan the structure of a news article. They propose a schema-source hierarchical structure for each document, propose and collect data for 8 schema structures and propose metrics to determine the most appropriate schema structure given a news article. They identify sources at sentence level and use the structure of sources to identify the most appropriate schema for a given article. They annotate a NewSource dataset using two annotations with moderate agreement (0.54 kappa). They train RoBERTa-based/T5-based/NLI model-based classifiers to identify source of given a sentence and schema of an article. They propose two metrics to evaluate their classifiers: conditional perplexity and posterior predictive likelihood. They evaluate their classifiers against a random baseline and a paragraph-level k-means baseline. They obtain improvements on some of the schema categories. From the previous version, they further add an expert-to-predictive model alignment evaluation to study the effectiveness and understand the limitations of the proposed approach of understanding journalistic planning. They conclude with an analysis how a particular schema might be more suited to explaining particular types of articles.

I reviewed the paper in the prior round as well. The new additional experiment is interesting and answers to an extent why the results in Table 3 are as such. The schema structures seem to be interesting while the utility of identifying the schema structures hasn’t been demonstrated in this paper, it is probably outside the scope of this work. Presentation issues such as consistency have been addressed to an extent. Writing could still be improved significantly. Often, sentences are unnecessarily convoluted and hard to understand (case in point L434-438).

Contributions:
1) An ontology of schema-source to explain new article structures.
2) Two approximate metrics (which don’t require gold annotation) that aim to evaluate schema assignment to articles.
3) A dataset of annotated source and schema assignments at sentence and article level respectively.
4) Empirical experiments that show that the classifiers trained on the data perform better than unsupervised baselines. Further evaluation which explores the limitations of trying to infer planning directly from the text of the article at fine-grained level.
reviews.strengths:
Strengths:
1) The proposed ontology is interesting and the dataset is a sizable contribution. From the analysis of classifier based results in Table 2, it seems that the ontology provides a reasonable discrimination between various types of news articles. IAA is moderately high.
2) Proposed metrics are interesting and cover interesting aspects of schema assignment to articles.
3) Empirical results show the usefulness of the annotated dataset in training classifiers for schema and source assignment for new articles. Additional experiments which aim to study the limitations of proposed schema structures add interesting insights to the empirical evaluation.
reviews.weaknesses:
Weaknesses:
1) Weak baselines: As mentioned in the previous version of the reviews, provided baselines are weak and sometimes are outperformed by the random baseline. While additional exploration was performed to understand why this happens, more sophisticated baselines could be explored, such as LLM-based baselines which evaluate the predictive capabilities of existing LLMs in inferring planning from the article text. While this is not a limiting factor to the main contribution of the paper, these could have greatly added to the usefulness of the study.
2) Issue with annotation protocol: Given that the annotation was performed in a trainer-trainee setting, it would be expected that the IAA is at least moderate. It would have been interesting to have at least two trainees and compute IAA between the two trainees. This issue would probably remain but this is a weakness of the paper nevertheless.
3) Missing details of the new experiment: The new experiment proposed in L454-458 could have been broken down by schema category. It would have been interesting to see if the under-performing categories correspond to categories where the random baseline outperforms as well.
